tagline.text: A white-sand sunset promenade beside Roxas Boulevard in Manila

location.label: Location
location.text: Manila Baywalk on Roxas Boulevard, Malate, Manila (near the US Embassy)

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱0–500 (free entry; per person including transport)

children.text: This is an artificial white beach of about 500 m, made by spreading crushed dolomite along one stretch of the Manila Baywalk. Entry is free and swimming is not allowed, so it is best for strolling and taking sunset photos around dusk.
Manila Bay Dolomite Beach is an artificial beach built along the Baywalk stretch of Roxas Boulevard in Malate, Manila. The first section runs about
from the Manila Yacht Club breakwater to near the US Embassy, and the plan called for a total length of about
and a width of about
. Two layers of ordinary sand were laid and covered with crushed dolomite, which is why the sand looks white. The dolomite is said to come from Alcoy in Cebu.

Its opening history is useful to know when planning a visit. It first opened on September 19–20, 2020 and then closed for expansion; after Typhoon Vamco (Ulysses) in November that year, garbage piled up, and the DENR replenished the sand in December. In April 2021 a new coat of dolomite sand was laid, and on July 18 it reopened without notice; in September an entrance arch reading "Manila Baywalk Dolomite Beach" was installed. It reopened again on October 17, and after an expansion closure it reopened on June 12, 2022, and the project was declared complete in October of that year. With so many closures, checking just before you go matters. The project has been controversial from the start: some senators opposed it in September 2020, mining at the dolomite source in Cebu was ordered halted, and in November 2025 a House representative backed a congressional probe. So think of this place less as a beach for swimming in the bay and more as a park for walking at sunset beside the city's sea.
The most important point is that swimming is prohibited. The government discourages entering the water because fecal coliform levels in Manila Bay are still far above the swimming standard (
100 MPN/100mL

for Class SB waters). Water quality has been reported to improve year by year, but it can worsen again after rain. So plan your visit around walking, sunset, photos and connecting to nearby sights along Roxas Boulevard.

The entrance to the sand area is on the US Embassy side of Roxas Boulevard, and the Baywalk promenade continues right beside it. Entry is free, and it is close to Malate, Ermita, Rizal Park and Intramuros, so it works well as a sunset stop at the end of a day of sightseeing in central Manila. Hours and rules have changed often, so check the latest announcements from the DENR and the City of Manila just before you go.

The sand, covered with crushed dolomite, looks bright against the usually grayish water of Manila Bay. You can walk along the sand area and look out over the bay to the horizon. The glare is strong at midday, so bring a hat and sunglasses.

The sunset over Manila Bay is one of the most famous views in the Philippines. In the dry season the sky often turns orange and purple. The sand area may close before the sun sets, so it is safest to arrive
30–40 minutes

before sunset. Sunset is cited at around 5:40 PM in November–January, after 6:05 PM in February–April and after 6:30 PM in May–July. It changes through the year, so check the sunset time for the day in an app.

The promenade along Roxas Boulevard fills with local families and couples from dusk into the evening. Street performers and vendors sometimes line it, so it is pleasant to stroll in the sea breeze even after the sand area closes.

blocks.title: City and sea in one frame

children.text: Looking from the beach toward the city, you can see the high-rises along Roxas Boulevard and ships on the bay together. It is a good composition for the typical Manila city sunset photo.

blocks.title: A short outing with family and kids

children.text: There is no entrance fee and the facilities are simple, so it is easy to drop in briefly. Swimming and water play are prohibited, so with children plan around walking on the sand and looking around. It is a good idea to wash hands after touching the sand.

blocks.title: A site of the Manila Bay rehabilitation project

children.text: This beach is both a symbol of the Manila Bay rehabilitation project and a subject of controversy. Signs and the surrounding scenery give you a chance to think about the environmental problems of a city sea, which makes it more than an ordinary beach visit.

blocks.title: Linking with Rizal Park and Intramuros

children.text: Rizal Park is about
1.8 km
to the north and Intramuros about
2.6 km
away. A popular plan is to see museums and the historic district by day, then come here for the sunset.

items.title: Sunset walk
items.subtitle: Arrive in the late afternoon and stay until sunset

children.text: Walk
10–15 minutes
from LRT-1 Pedro Gil Station or Roxas Boulevard to the Baywalk promenade. First stroll the promenade to get a feel for the place.
Pass the bag check at the sand-area entrance (US Embassy side) and go in. Check the signs for the limit on single-use plastics and the current rules.
Walk on the sand, take photos and pick your sunset spot. It is best to claim a spot before the crowds arrive.
Enjoy the reddest sky as the sun touches the horizon. Follow the exit instructions before the sand area closes.
Return to the promenade, have dinner in the Malate or Ermita dining area and take a Grab back to your hotel.

In November–January the sun sets early, so you may not see the sunset from the sand area and may have to watch it from the promenade. Check the hours locally. Waits to enter can be long on weekend and holiday afternoons, so weekdays are recommended. It has closed over some holiday periods in the past, so check ahead.

items.title: Half-day Manila city route
items.subtitle: From Rizal Park on foot to sunset

children.text: Start at Rizal Park and look around the National Museum area and the park.
Move on to Intramuros and walk the walls and the San Agustin Church area.
Go to the Baywalk by Grab or taxi.
Finish by watching the sunset from the Baywalk promenade or the Dolomite Beach.

From Makati or BGC, set the Roxas Boulevard Baywalk area as your destination in a Grab or taxi. Allow plenty of time because of traffic.
A convenient Grab drop-off is near Remedios Street on Roxas Boulevard.
From LRT-1 Pedro Gil Station it is about
10–15 minutes
on foot to the Baywalk, about
10–12 minutes
from United Nations Avenue Station and about
15–20 minutes
from Vito Cruz Station.
You can also take a tricycle from the station to Roxas Boulevard. One 2021 guide gave about
, but confirm the fare locally.
Tell the jeepney driver "Roxas Boulevard, Malate" or "Baywalk Dolomite Beach."
From PITX, buses toward Quiapo, Lawton and Monumento are said to pass along Roxas Boulevard, but routes and fares change, so confirm locally.

The dry season from November to May is a good time to visit. December–February in particular is relatively cool and clear, which is good for sunset photos. The sun sets between 5:30 and 6:00 PM in this period, so be sure to check the sand area's hours.

In the rainy and typhoon season from June to October, entry may be restricted or the beach closed because of waves and rain. Water quality can temporarily worsen after rain, so check PAGASA weather bulletins.

There is no lodging at the beach itself; use the hotels and guesthouses in the nearby Malate and Ermita areas. The location pairs well with a day of Manila sightseeing, and some lodgings are within walking distance of the Baywalk. Prices vary greatly by season, so check booking sites.

Roxas Boulevard and the Malate streets have many Korean restaurants, Filipino restaurants and cafes. Food may be restricted inside the sand area, so it is better to eat on the promenade side. It can get dark along the roads at night, so use Grab to get around.

Many Korean travelers put this stop last when they cover central Manila in a day. Walk Rizal Park, the National Museum and Intramuros by day, then move over around 4:30 PM to arrive near sunset. Think of the sand area not as a place to stay long but as somewhere you enter, take photos, stroll and leave, and your schedule will be easier.
Opening hours differ by source. They are usually given as 6 AM to 6 PM, but it is known to close on Thursdays for maintenance in many accounts, so confirm locally.
Arrive at least
30–40 minutes
before sunset to get in and find a spot.
The bag check may restrict single-use plastics. Travel light.
There is only one entrance. Look for the entrance on Roxas Boulevard on the US Embassy side.
Swimming and water play are prohibited. You do not need swimwear; wear sandals or sneakers.
Hang your phone and camera around your neck or hold them, and keep your wallet in a front pocket. Watch for pickpockets when it is crowded.
Mosquitoes can be plentiful around dusk, so bring repellent.
Use Grab for evening trips and choose a pickup point on a busy main road.
When it reopened in 2021, there were time limits and age limits on visits. If crowds build, time limits may apply now too, so follow the instructions at the entrance.
Swimming is prohibited because of Manila Bay's water quality. Do not enter the water or play in it.
Water quality is said to be poorer for
24–48 hours
after rain.
The Department of Health has said that crushed dolomite dust can irritate the respiratory system. If you have asthma, consider wearing a mask.
In typhoon season the sand can be washed away or the beach may close.

In July 2025 the Metropolitan Manila Development Authority (MMDA) claimed the beach worsens flooding by blocking drainage, and the DENR was reported to be seeking solutions. The facility may change, so check the latest news.
The sand area closes at night and the promenade quiets down, so avoid visiting late.
The whole Manila Bay sunset area that the Dolomite Beach belongs to. It continues along the Baywalk.
